title: Same rule, five test groups
hook: One unchanging rule, five held-out groups. How far apart can the scores land?

knows: that a model is scored on held-out data it was not fitted to
that a small test set is noisy
doesNotKnow: how much one held-out slice's score can swing
that k-fold cross-validation rotates the held-out group so every point is used once

misconception: Whichever test slice you picked gives the model's accuracy.
objective: The learner can say that scores on different held-out groups differ even for a fixed rule, and that averaging over k folds uses every point once and gives a steadier number.

claims.text: The 20 points, their labels and the rule 'say 1 if x > 0.5' are a toy: exactly 4 labels (20%) are flipped, and the rule is fixed, not trained. Labelled 'Toy data · fixed rule, not trained' on the stage.
claims.source: Brief 43 in company/domains/briefs/ai.md, adapted: the brief used random 20% flips with an LCG; this build flips exactly 4 of 20 so the answer does not depend on the seed. MODEL block in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: On the stage's split the five folds score 100%, 75%, 100%, 50% and 75%: a spread of 50 percentage points; their mean is 80%, the same as the 16 of 20 dots the rule gets right.
claims.source: SCORES, MEAN, RIGHT_ALL in Demo.tsx with mulberry32(seed 1), the first seed, untuned (flipped points 3, 6, 11, 13). node re-run: [100, 75, 100, 50, 75], mean 80. The mean equals 16/20 for every seed, since equal folds partition the points. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): Own node reimplementation (kit mulberry32 seed 1, Fisher-Yates): flipped points {3,6,11,13}; folds [100,75,100,50,75], spread 50, mean 80 = 16/20 (equal folds partition the points). Reveal and readouts print SCORES/MEAN from the same model.

claims.text: With 4 wrong labels in five folds of 4 dots, the fold scores can never all be equal, so two folds always differ by at least one dot, which is 25 percentage points.
claims.source: Derivation: equal scores need an equal number of wrong labels per fold, impossible for 4 across 5 folds. A one-dot difference in a fold of 4 is 25 percentage points. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 16): Derivation: equal fold scores need equal wrong labels per fold, 4/5 is not an integer, so two folds differ by >= 1 dot = 25 points in a fold of 4. node seeds 1-1000: spread 25 in 253, 50 in 671, 75 in 76, never below 25. Support is labelled 'simulation' but this is a derivation; non-blocking.

claims.text: k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k groups, holds out each group once, and averages the k scores, so every point is used for testing exactly once.
claims.source: Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., §7.10 (K-fold cross-validation).

recall.question: A model scores 95% on one held-out slice of 20 examples. A colleague's 5-fold cross-validation gives 82%. Which number better describes the model, and why?
options: 95%: it is the real test result
82%: it averages five held-out groups, so one lucky slice counts less
Neither: they disagree, so both are meaningless
recall.why: One small held-out slice can swing a long way by luck of which points land in it. Rotating the held-out group and averaging uses every point once.
